meta.descriptionEn: For 53 years, a 305-metre dish hidden in a Puerto Rican sinkhole was the largest single-aperture radio telescope on Earth. It tracked asteroids, probed the ionosphere, joined the hunt for alien signals, and in 1974 beamed a message of 1,679 bits toward a star cluster 25,000 light-years away. Then, in 2020, cables began to snap. Why did a giant built to last fail so suddenly? What did investigators discover about zinc, loads and hidden weaknesses? And what is rising on the site today? Join us for the full story of Arecibo, from its Cold War origins to its final morning, in Urdu and English.

articleEn: On the morning of December 1, 2020, Puerto Rico seemed to be having an ordinary day. It was about 7:56 a.m., and a quiet hung over the Arecibo Observatory. Then the remaining support cables attached to one of the towers suddenly snapped. It all happened very fast, and the scene was changed forever.

The receiver platform, which hung 150 meters above the dish, fell and tore straight through the enormous reflector. In the same jolt, the upper parts of the support towers broke off, and some nearby buildings suffered partial damage. One thing brought some relief: nobody was hurt in the entire incident.

This was the telescope that had been the world's largest single-aperture telescope for 53 years, and now it had collapsed. So why did this giant machine fall? What did it give to science during its life? And what is left there today? Interestingly, the observatory's other facilities, such as the small radio telescope, the LIDAR facility and the visitor center, kept working after the disaster.
This story is not about a single accident. It is a tale of decades of dreams, science and hard struggle. Let's begin from the start.

articleEn: Let's go back to the 1950s. ARPA, an agency of the United States Department of Defense, was trying to solve a difficult problem: how could missiles be detected in the Earth's ionosphere, the upper layer of the atmosphere that the ordinary eye cannot reach? The job needed a very large ionospheric radar probe, an instrument able to study that layer high above the ground. This is where Cornell University enters the story.

On November 6, 1959, Cornell signed a contract with ARPA. Its purpose was development studies, meaning early research and planning, for a large-scale ionospheric radar probe. A university and a defense agency were together shaping the dream of a machine that looks at the sky. But the plan did not stay limited to the ionosphere. Alongside ionospheric study, it was also built as a general-purpose radio telescope. It was not just a radar; it was to become a major means of listening to radio signals from the universe.

Construction began in September 1960, in the Barrio Esperanza area of the town of Arecibo, Puerto Rico. The work went on for about three years, and the plan that had been on paper slowly took shape on the ground. Then came November 1, 1963, when the telescope and its supporting observatory were formally inaugurated. At that time it was called the Arecibo Ionospheric Observatory, a name that showed its first purpose was to understand the ionosphere. Later the facility also became known as the National Astronomy and Ionosphere Center, or NAIC. The story of that change comes later.

Today the observatory is owned by the US National Science Foundation, or NSF, though it was not so at the start. While the project was under ARPA and the Department of Defense, it was tied to the need to catch missiles in the upper atmosphere. But in science, a machine often goes far beyond its original purpose, and that is what happened with Arecibo. Its original aim was studying the ionosphere, yet the same telescope went on to play a part in radio astronomy, radar astronomy and SETI.
But how was something so big built? What was its structure? In the next part, we look inside this giant.

articleEn: Now to the giant's construction. The heart of the Arecibo Telescope was its main collecting dish, shaped like an upturned dome or bowl. The dish was 1,000 feet, or 305 meters, in diameter. Its surface was spherical, with a radius of curvature of 869 feet, about 265 meters. This was the signature of its design.

The dish was not built on level ground. It was constructed inside a natural karst sinkhole. Karst is a geological process that creates natural depressions, and in Arecibo one such hollow became the home of the dish. The surface was not a solid sheet of metal. It was made of 38,778 perforated aluminum panels, panels with small holes in them. Each panel measured about 3 feet by 7 feet, roughly 1 meter by 2 meters. Thousands of such pieces were joined to form the giant bowl. All the panels rested on a mesh of steel cables, so the whole dish was really held up by a strong net of wires. Below the dish, shade-tolerant vegetation grew on the ground.

Then there was the part that did the real work. Above the dish, a cable-mounted steerable receiver hung in the air, together with several radar transmitters that sent signals out into space. This whole system was set 150 meters, or 492 feet, above the dish, about the height of a very tall building. Holding instruments up at such a height with cables was a major engineering challenge. The cables were held by support towers. Keep this in mind, because these cables and towers become the most important part of the final chapters of this story.

What made Arecibo special was that it could both send signals through its radar transmitters and listen to radio waves coming from far away. The structure was completed in 1963, and for 53 years it remained the world's largest single-aperture telescope, meaning a telescope with one large dish.

Then in July 2016, China's Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope, or FAST, appeared and surpassed it. Interestingly, FAST's dish is also built in a natural karst sinkhole, though its diameter is 500 meters. That was the structure of Arecibo. articleEn: On October 1, 1969, the Department of Defense handed the observatory over to the National Science Foundation, or NSF. After that, Cornell University was given the job of managing it. By September 1971 the NSF had given it a new name, the National Astronomy and Ionosphere Center, or NAIC. It also received the status of a federally funded research and development center, shortened to FFRDC. In this period NASA also began to provide funding together with the NSF, because of NASA's planetary radar mission. Remember that the project began for a specific ARPA purpose. Now its owner had changed, and the NSF had given its management to Cornell. The observatory that began with a question about the ionosphere was now serving many kinds of science.

One job of the telescope was radar astronomy: sending out a radio signal and listening to its echo. Another was radio astronomy, listening to radio waves from the sky. The telescope was also part of SETI programs. NASA used it as well to track Near-Earth objects, bodies passing close to Earth.

The observatory's role in understanding Solar System bodies was so notable that an asteroid was named after it. It is called 4337 Arecibo. Steven J. Ostro gave it that name, because of the observatory's services in characterizing Solar System objects. A rock in the sky named after an observatory on the ground is a great honor for any institution.

One part of the observatory was made for the general public. In 1997 the Ángel Ramos Foundation Visitor Center opened there. It holds interactive exhibits about the telescope, astronomy and atmospheric sciences. It is named in honor of Ángel Ramos, owner of the newspaper El Mundo and founder of Telemundo. The foundation gave half of the money, and the rest came from private donations and Cornell University. The aim was to raise public interest in astronomy and space. Together with the Caribbean Astronomical Society, the center also holds Astronomical Nights throughout the year, with talks on topics such as exoplanets and Comet ISON.

So the place was doing many jobs at once: ionosphere research, tracking objects in space, and connecting the public with science. But perhaps Arecibo's most famous story is something else: a message sent toward the stars in 1974. What was that message?

articleEn: On November 16, 1974, a ceremony was held for the remodeling of the Arecibo Telescope, and on that occasion a special message was sent into space. It is called the Arecibo message. It was an interstellar radio message carrying basic information about humans and Earth. Its target was the globular cluster Messier 13, or M13, chosen because, at that time and from that place, it was a large and relatively close group of stars in the sky. M13 is about 25,000 light-years from Earth, so even at the speed of light the message will take at least 25,000 years to arrive.

The message was created by a team of Cornell and Arecibo scientists, including Frank Drake, James C. G. Walker, Linda M. French and Richard Isaacman. Carl Sagan and some others also contributed. It is worth remembering that its purpose was to demonstrate human technology, not a serious attempt at conversation. The message was made of 1,679 binary digits, about 210 bytes. It was sent at a frequency of 2,380 MHz with 450 kW of power, once, through frequency shifting, at 10 bits per second. The whole broadcast was over in less than three minutes.

Why 1,679? Because it is a semiprime, the product of two prime numbers. Those two numbers make a grid of 73 rows and 23 columns. If you try 23 rows and 73 columns, you get meaningless marks. The message was divided into seven parts. At the top were the numbers one to ten in binary. Next came the atomic numbers of the elements that make up DNA: hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and phosphorus. After that came the chemical formulas of the DNA nucleotides.

The fourth part showed the double helix of DNA and the estimated number of nucleotides in the human genome, which was then thought to be about 4.3 billion. Today we know the human genome has about 3.2 billion base pairs, so the 1974 estimate turned out to differ from current knowledge. The fifth part held a human figure, along with the height of the average man, about 5 feet 9 inches, and the human population at that time, about 4 billion.

The sixth part was a map of the Solar System showing nine planets including Pluto. Earth was raised up to show that the message was coming from there. At the end came a picture of the telescope and its diameter written in binary. The number was 2,430, and multiplied by the 126 mm wavelength it gives about 306 meters. After being sent, the message had a 25,000-year journey ahead of it, and by then the center of M13 will have moved from its place.

Now an interesting twist. In 2001 a crop circle appeared in Hampshire, UK, near the Chilbolton radio telescope, and it was also called the Arecibo answer. It was a near copy of the original message with some differences. The DNA part included silicon, and instead of the human figure there was a big-headed figure. The SETI Institute said there was no evidence of any extraterrestrial source and called it highly improbable. In other words, it turned out to be a hoax.
Finally, a question: could someone who knows nothing of the message recognize it in the signal? A 2025 LCC score from Mahon correctly identified the 73 by 23 aspect ratio.

articleEn: The Arecibo message was only one part of a larger story. The telescope was also involved in the search for an answer to a question: are we alone in the universe? This search is called SETI, the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence. Its aim is to find any intelligent signal or evidence coming from space.

In 1960, Cornell astronomer Frank Drake carried out the first modern SETI experiment, called Project Ozma. Using the 26-meter radio telescope at Green Bank, West Virginia, Drake listened to the stars Tau Ceti and Epsilon Eridani. He found nothing of interest. Then on August 15, 1977, Jerry Ehman, working with Ohio State University's Big Ear telescope, saw an unusually strong signal. He circled it on the printout and wrote "Wow!" in the margin, which is why it is called the Wow! signal. Some regard it as the best candidate so far, but it was not found again in many further searches. The SETI Institute also does not officially accept it as extraterrestrial in origin, because it could not be confirmed.

How did Arecibo become part of this search? In 1992 NASA's Microwave Observing Program, or MOP, began, and it was to use the Arecibo telescope. But MOP met opposition in Congress and was ended a year after it started. In 1995 the SETI Institute revived it with private funding as Project Phoenix, led by Jill Tarter. Phoenix made observations from 1995 to March 2004 at Parkes, Green Bank and Arecibo, studying about 1,000 nearby Sun-like stars.

Then came SERENDIP, started in 1979 by the Berkeley SETI Research Center. It collected data alongside other astronomers' observations. SERENDIP VI was installed on both the Arecibo and Green Bank telescopes in 2014-2015. SERENDIP data was analyzed by volunteers of SETI@home, which began in May 1999. By June 28, 2009, it had more than 180,000 active participants, with more than 290,000 computers taking part.

After so many years of searching, what was the result? The truth is that no confirmed evidence of alien intelligence has been found to this day. This silence is the root of the Fermi paradox. Enrico Fermi said in the 1950s that if advanced civilizations were common, they should be detectable somehow. There are many explanations. One says intelligent life is very rare. Another says perhaps we are not looking for the right signs.

SETI also draws criticism. According to a 2009 Nature editorial, it is not a falsifiable experiment, because radio silence does not prove that aliens do not exist. Another debate concerns active messaging, meaning sending messages ourselves. Stephen Hawking said doing so could be dangerous and that we should lay low. Jill Tarter disagrees. In her view such civilizations would be more cooperative, though the time has not yet come for active SETI.

In July 2016 FAST moved ahead. According to its website, it can reach out to 28 light-years, while Arecibo's distance was 18. So what happened to Arecibo? Its next chapter hides years of mounting pressure.

articleEn: Arecibo's financial story was not easy. In the early 2000s, NASA ended its funding for the observatory. Then in 2006 the NSF signaled that it would reduce funding, and that if no other source was found, the observatory could even be decommissioned. After this decision, academics and politicians lobbied to avoid closure, aiming to save the observatory from shutting down. Meanwhile the NSF's attention was moving toward newer instruments. From about 2006, funding for the telescope kept shrinking, even though experts continued to appeal to Congress.

In 2011 things improved somewhat. NASA promised funding again for the study of near-Earth objects. That same year the NSF removed Arecibo from the FFRDC list, which meant the observatory could now seek funding from a wider range of sources. Another big change followed: a team led by SRI International took over as site operator in place of Cornell. The institution that had run the telescope for decades now stepped back.

But the problems were not over; a storm was coming. In 2017 Hurricane Maria struck and damaged the telescope. Several earlier hurricanes had also affected parts of it. Repairs on a small budget were already hard, and now the damage had grown, and the NSF once again proposed closing the observatory.

Then a consortium led by the University of Central Florida, or UCF, stepped forward. It offered to run the observatory and take on a large share of the costs. In 2018 the NSF made the UCF consortium the new site operator. However, no specific actions or funding were announced on that occasion.

It is important to understand that this was not a problem of a single day. Years of low funding, storm damage and changing operators were all going on together. Meanwhile the telescope kept doing its work. It continued to be used for radar astronomy, radio astronomy and SETI, and NASA used it for detecting near-Earth objects. But deep inside, something very dangerous was going on. Then 2020 came, and one cable changed everything. That story begins now.

articleEn: In August 2020 came Arecibo's first major warning. One of the telescope's auxiliary cables broke. It was one of the receiver's support cables. Sources differ slightly on the date, with one saying August 10 and another August 6, so we will simply say August 2020. The break weakened the support structure of the suspended platform, and the dish was damaged too.

The matter did not end there. In November 2020 came a second blow, when a main cable broke. Here too the dates differ, with some sources saying November 6 and others November 7. After two cable breaks, the NSF had to decide whether to repair the telescope or to bring it down safely. In November 2020 the NSF concluded that decommissioning was safer than trying to repair it. According to the announcement, the telescope was to be taken down by controlled demolition, while the rest of the observatory's facilities were to keep running. The fate of a great telescope had been decided, but its end did not come in a planned way.

Then came the morning of December 1, 2020. At about 7:56 local time, the remaining support cables connected to one tower suddenly failed. As soon as they did, the receiver platform fell and struck the dish. The upper parts of the support towers broke as well, and some other buildings suffered partial damage. But the most important point is that nobody was injured in the incident.

NSF officials had said in 2020 that they wanted to reopen the remaining observatory facilities soon, and that they were also considering building a new telescope instrument at the site. So the telescope fell by itself before the controlled demolition could happen. The machine that had been the world's largest single-aperture telescope for 53 years was gone very quickly.
The question still remained: why did the cables break? To find the answer, a major investigation led by NASA began.

articleEn: Now the biggest question: why did the cables fail? NASA carried out a wide-ranging failure investigation and released a technical bulletin for industry with its findings. The conclusion was that low socket design margin and very high sustained loading exposed an unexpected weakness against zinc creep. According to the report, the result was long-term cumulative damage: harm that built up slowly until progressive zinc and wire failure occurred. Remember that the environment also played a role, as the investigation mentioned both zinc creep and environmental conditions.

In 2024 the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine published its definitive report, titled Failure Analysis of the Arecibo Observatory 305-Meter Telescope Collapse. It cited many findings of earlier investigations. It discussed how high-energy output and zinc wire rope interact, a effect called brooming. The report also raised another issue: the gap between the original design standards of the 1980s and later advances in wind load engineering.

Now Arecibo's future. In 2020 the NSF was considering building a new instrument, but in 2022 it was announced that the telescope would not be rebuilt. It was decided instead to build an educational facility on the site. The next year the NSF chose a consortium of four institutions: Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, the University of Puerto Rico's Río Piedras Campus, and the University of the Sacred Heart. The consortium will run an education center called Arecibo C3, whose full name is Arecibo Center for Culturally Relevant and Inclusive Science Education, Computational Skills, and Community Engagement.

The observatory has not ended. A small radio telescope, the LIDAR facility and the Visitor Center kept running after the collapse. The 12-meter radio telescope was built for VLBI, and LIDAR research continues after the collapse.

What do we learn from this story? In large structures, design margin, constant load and environment cannot be ignored. Another lesson is about funding: the NSF's attention moved to newer instruments, storms increased the damage, and pressure remained on a small budget. The open question is how to keep such big instruments safe, and who will carry forward the science that Arecibo began.

Support towers ke upri hissay kat gaye, aur kuch imaraton ko bhi nuqsan pohancha. Acchi baat yeh thi ke kisi ko chot nahin aayi. Ajeeb baat yeh hai ke NSF pehle hi is telescope ko decommission karne ka elaan kar chuka tha. To phir cables tootin kyun? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

shorts.titleEn: The Message Humans Sent to M13 in 1974
shorts.text: کیا انسان نے کبھی خلا میں اپنا پیغام بھیجا ہے؟ 16 November 1974 کو Arecibo Telescope کی remodeling کی تقریب میں ایک radio message بھیجا گیا۔ نشانہ تھا globular cluster M13، جو زمین سے تقریباً 25,000 light-years دور ہے۔ یعنی پیغام کو وہاں پہنچنے میں کم از کم 25,000 سال لگیں گے۔ اس میں صرف 1,679 bits تھے۔ ان میں 1 سے 10 تک گنتی، DNA کے elements، انسان کی تصویر اور Solar System کا graphic تھا۔ اسے Frank Drake سمیت Cornell اور Arecibo کے scientists کی ٹیم نے بنایا۔ لیکن 1,679 ہی کیوں؟ اس نمبر میں ایسا کیا راز تھا کہ غلط ترتیب سے سجانے پر سب کچھ بیکار ہو جاتا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya insan ne kabhi khala mein apna paigham bheja hai? 16 November 1974 ko Arecibo Telescope ki remodeling ki taqreeb mein aik radio message bheja gaya. Nishana tha globular cluster M13, jo zameen se taqriban 25,000 light-years door hai. Yani paigham ko wahan pohanchne mein kam az kam 25,000 saal lagenge. Is mein sirf 1,679 bits thay. In mein 1 se 10 tak ginti, DNA ke elements, insan ki tasveer aur Solar System ka graphic tha. Ise Frank Drake samet Cornell aur Arecibo ke scientists ki team ne banaya. Lekin 1,679 hi kyun? Is number mein aisa kya raaz tha ke galat tarteeb se sajane par sab kuch bekaar ho jata? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: In 1974 the Arecibo message was sent toward star cluster M13, about 25,000 light-years away. It held 1,679 bits about humanity and Earth.

shorts.titleEn: Two Cable Breaks That Doomed a 305 m Telescope
shorts.text: دو cables نے 305 meter کے ایک عظیم telescope کی قسمت لکھ دی۔ August 2020 میں Arecibo کی ایک auxiliary cable ٹوٹ گئی۔ Dates پر sources میں فرق ہے: ایک جگہ 10 August لکھا ہے، دوسری جگہ 6 August۔ پھر November 2020 میں ایک main cable بھی ٹوٹ گئی، اور یہاں بھی 6 اور 7 November کا فرق ہے۔ ان breaks نے receiver کے support structure کی مضبوطی خطرے میں ڈال دی اور dish کو نقصان پہنچا۔ NSF کے سامنے سوال تھا: مرمت کریں یا محفوظ طریقے سے telescope کو decommission کریں؟ November 2020 میں NSF نے فیصلہ کیا کہ repair سے بہتر decommission کرنا محفوظ ہے۔ لیکن کیا telescope کو controlled demolition کا وقت مل سکا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Do cables ne 305 meter ke aik azeem telescope ki kismat likh di. August 2020 mein Arecibo ki aik auxiliary cable toot gayi. Dates par sources mein farq hai: aik jagah 10 August likha hai, doosri jagah 6 August. Phir November 2020 mein aik main cable bhi toot gayi, aur yahan bhi 6 aur 7 November ka farq hai. In breaks ne receiver ke support structure ki mazbooti khatray mein daal di aur dish ko nuqsan pohancha. NSF ke samne sawal tha: marammat karein ya mehfooz tareeqay se telescope ko decommission karein? November 2020 mein NSF ne faisla kiya ke repair se behtar decommission karna mehfooz hai. Lekin kya telescope ko controlled demolition ka waqt mil saka? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: Two cable breaks in 2020 damaged Arecibo's dish and its support structure. NSF then chose decommissioning over repair as the safer option.
